newsitem.title: FRANCE: Alcatel aims to triple GSM set sales.
newsitem.headline: Alcatel aims to triple GSM set sales.

text.p: Alcatel Alsthom on Tuesday announced a new familiy of GSM mobile phones and said it aimed to triple its unit sales in 1997.

Patrick Liot, vice president of Alcatel's terminals devision, told a news conference that the "One Touch Pro" GSM phone was, at 15 millimetres the flattest in the market and had an icon-based navigating system, allowing the user to browse to the menu with a track-ball kind of button.
"It means to mobile telecoms what Windows means to computers," he told a news conference on the eve of the GSM World Congress in this Mediterrenean resort.
He said that while Alcatel sold one million GSM sets, made at its Laval plant in France, it aimed to sell three million terminals in 1997.

"This will give us a market share of 12 percent, an increase of five points," he said. In 1996, Alcatel had a world GSM market share of six percent and in Europe its share was eight percent, Liot said, basing this on Dataquest figures.

Alain Bravo, chairman of the mobile communication division, said that in infrastructure, Alcatel had a market share in GSM/DCS of 12 percent at the end of 1996 and aimed to grow it by two points every year.
"My goal is very simple. In the year 2000 I want to have 20 percent of the market," he told Reuters.
Alcatel currently ranks fourth in the digital mobile telecoms market, after Motorola Inc, AB LM Ericsson and Nokia Oy.
"We aim to be in the top three," Bravo said.
Alcatel said it was going to focus on offering value added services to GSM operators.
"An operator wants to get a higher return on investment and a user want to have services that go beyond basic telephony," Bravo said.
An example of such a value added service was a pact in Britain between Cellway and Barclays Bank Plc, offering mobile phones with a special button to contact a bank branch.
But future services will be more sophisticated and Alcatel plans to roll out a number of these services in the coming year.
An example of this is a deal with private U.S. company Unwired Planet in which the Redwood Shores, CA, located firm will provide its UP.Browser client applications on GSM phones.
"The three hottest markets at the moment are mobile telecommunications, personal computers and the Internet. We thought we'd combine two of them by bringing Internet to the mobile phone," Liot said.
Asked about a statement by Ericsson that GSM handset prices could fall by 20 to 25 percent in 1997, Liot said the statement was "aggressive".
"Prices were down by 10 to 15 percent in 1996. Now Ericsson is adding 10 points. That is very aggressive, very Ericsson, aimed at defending their strong position," Liot said.
"It's fine with me, it means there will be good competition."
Alcatel is a relatively late arrival to mobile telecommunications and does not enjoy the brand recognition of the top three companies.
Bravo said that this was mainly due to the fact that Alcatel had not been in analogue mobile communications previously.
"Those guys started with analogue systems in the 1970s. We came with GSM in the 1980s. It took some time to acquire the competences but we are on a par now," Bravo told Reuters.
Alcatel's GSM/DCS system sales were 5.1 billion francs in 1996. It did not communicate is terminal sales.
